transcript.answer_text:
Jesus was the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we hold to be his birthplace. Our deepest devotion has the shape of that choice: the Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough, and so wealth, rank, and comfort are things we lay down to come near him.

The land itself we treated as a kind of witness. Our founders crossed the sea to live inside it. More than three and a half centuries stood between us and the events - no one among us had ever known an eyewitness, and no one pretended otherwise. Our confidence stood on three things: the apostles' writings as received, the unbroken worship of the churches, and the places themselves. We knew the resurrection really happened from the writings we trusted enough to spend a life correcting. We knew it from a hope strong enough that people gave away fortunes on it.

We worked over the text of scripture word by word, because we believed the writings were the true treasure handed down, worth a lifetime of exactness. The Gospels and the whole of scripture were copied, compared, corrected, and translated from the Hebrew we held truest - the Hebraica veritas. To the scholar among us, Jesus is the Word, worth that lifetime of labor to translate truly.

To the virgin, Jesus is the Bridegroom - and lifelong consecrated virginity, what we called virginitas, we held as the highest form of Christian life open to a woman. To the penitent he is the doctor who receives the broken. His death is our redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

Then you have already done a hard and honest thing, saying it plainly. We will not answer you with an argument. We will tell you what we actually had: hearts divided, wounded, or publicly ruined - and not turned away for it.

Our teacher Jerome told this against himself. In a dream he stood before the Judge and was accused of being a follower of Cicero and not of Christ, since where his treasure was, there his heart was too. He counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God, not the end of it. The dream was his own telling - we cannot verify the fever or the voice from heaven, only that he carried the tension between the books he loved and the book he served, and that he made it the story of his own turning.

We also remember Fabiola. Her marriage had failed. She married again while her first husband lived - against what we teach - and all Rome knew it. When her second husband died, she did not defend herself: “Who would believe it? After her second husband died -- at a time when most widows shake off the yoke of restraint and grow careless, taking more liberty than ever... -- Fabiola instead came to herself. It was then that she put on sackcloth to make public confession of her wrongdoing. It was then, before all Rome, in the basilica that had once belonged to Lateranus (who died by Caesar's sword), that she stood in the ranks of the penitents. Bishop, presbyters, and people watched, weeping to see her weep, as she showed her disheveled hair, pale features, soiled hands, and unwashed neck.”

She came in sackcloth and was received, and she spent the rest of her life carrying the sick in from the streets with her own hands.

We will not dress this up as an argument. It is only this: the door was opened to the divided and the broken among us, and what they could not yet believe, we helped them live toward.

Jesus is God the Son, of one being with the Father. The Trinity - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God - is simply the faith of the church, which we defended against every heresy we fought. We were born after the great council had settled that, and we never treated it as negotiable. To us it would be strange to hear it asked as an open question.

This is what we confessed, but we will tell you plainly what that means about what we left behind. We did not write our own treatise on the Trinity. What we have to give you is not a worked-out theology but a confession already received - the creed settled at the council of Nicaea, before our time began, which we held as the faith of the whole church. When we fought, we fought for that faith against those who questioned it. The fight over Origen's teachings - the Origenist controversy - turned on exactly this kind of question, and it tore our oldest friendship apart. Jerome and Rufinus had been friends for decades, and the rupture between them over what Origen had taught about the Son was doctrinal, personal, and political at once. We cannot tell you where doctrine ended and wounded pride began, because the record shows both, and both were real.

We spoke of Christ's death as redemption, ransom, and healing: the physician entering our sickness, the debt of sin paid. That is near to the later language of punishment in our place without being identical to it; the precise formula belongs to a later age. And the devotion was not abstract. A virgin among us addressed him as her Bridegroom, a penitent as her physician, and a dying woman greeted his birthplace by name. Jerome wrote to Eustochium that when she prays, she is speaking to the Bridegroom, and when she reads, he is speaking to her: “Always let the privacy of your chamber guard you; always let the Bridegroom delight with you within. Do you pray? You speak to the Bridegroom. Do you read? He speaks to you. When sleep overtakes you, he will come behind and put his hand through the opening of the door, and your heart shall be moved for him; and you will awake and rise up and say: 'I am sick with love.'”

Personal Lord and Savior was not our phrase, but the devotion those words carry is close kin to what that modern phrase means.

We held that the God we worshipped is one God in three persons - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - and that was the settled faith of the church, which we never treated as negotiable. The Son is of one being with the Father, not made or lesser, and we defended that against every heresy we fought. But you have not asked us for a creed. You have asked what God was like - what kind of God we met in our own lives.

The God we knew was the one who entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. That entry shapes everything we can tell you about his character. The Lord of all things chose weakness, poverty, and a cave for animals as the door into our world. So we understood him as the one who draws near in what is low, not in what is grand. And we followed that understanding with our lives: wealth and rank are laid down, not taken up, to come near him.

We knew him also as judge. We believed in real judgment and real punishment, and we did not soften that. But we were not consistent executors of our own severity. The same voice that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen. We held that no one is without sin, and that God's grace is needed not once but in every act. Against those who taught that a person can live perfectly without sin, we answered that everyone needs that grace, every day.

And we knew him in catastrophe. Rome fell in our own lifetime. Our teacher's voice stuck in his throat as he dictated, and he wrote that famine outran the sword: “My voice sticks in my throat, and sobs choke me as I dictate. The city that had captured the whole world was itself captured. Worse: famine got there before the sword, and only a few citizens were left to be taken prisoner.”

Years later, our own monastery burned at the hands of fellow Christians. The God we met in those fires was the one who lets the weeping happen and does not call it faithlessness. Our comfort letters argue and mourn at once. We gave our answers - judgment on a proud city, reward stored up, the dead safe with Christ - and we gave our sobs with them. We kept both on purpose.

One more thing. The Hebrew text of scripture - we called it hebraica veritas - we held to be the truest text, standing closer to what God said than the Greek the church had long used. That conviction was Jerome's own, and it was resisted. But for us it meant this: God's word is worth a lifetime of exactness, worth learning a new alphabet for, worth correcting every inherited translation against. The character of God we knew was one that rewarded that labor - not with ease, but with truth.

When belief was disputed among us, no single court decided it. The record shows exactly how messy that was. In our great internal fight, both sides appealed to everything at once: to scripture, to the councils' faith, to the bishop of Rome, to the bishop of Alexandria, to local bishops, and to the judgment of whoever was reading. The fight ended less by a verdict than by exhaustion and death.

The Hebraica veritas - the conviction that the Hebrew text of scripture is the truest text - shows this most clearly. Jerome worked from it for decades, translating and correcting the Latin Bible. Augustine objected that abandoning the Septuagint's received authority risked the church's continuity and unity. At Oea a congregation revolted over one changed word in Jonah. Jerome held his course. In his preface to Samuel and Kings he wrote: “This preface can serve as a "helmeted" introduction to all the books that we turn from Hebrew into Latin. It is meant to assure us that whatever is not found in our list must be placed among the Apocryphal writings.”

That argument never closed. Both men died with it unresolved.

They show the process by showing the fight.

We were textual ascetics. Reading scripture was not separate from renunciation - renuntiatio, our word for the deliberate giving-up of wealth and rank - it was the same discipline. We believed the Hebrew text of scripture carried the truth closest to what God said - the Hebraica veritas - and we spent decades correcting the Latin against it, book by book. The conviction behind the whole labor was this: the Hebrew stands closer to the inspired origin than the Greek translation the church had long used. That principle organized everything - the years of study, the translation itself, and the running fight we had to conduct in its defense.

The labor was formation. Correcting a word against the Hebrew was as much a discipline as fasting. We did not treat the text passively. Paula learned Hebrew so thoroughly that she could chant the psalms in it without a trace of Latin accent. Her daughter learned it after her. That arguing was the formation.

The method itself was one man's work, and we can only reconstruct it from what he wrote in his prefaces - the praefationes where he defended his approach book by book. We had books - the bibliotheca he gathered and worked from, though we cannot tell you its size or even confirm he used that word for it. We suppose he worked in some dedicated space, though no source names a scriptorium for us. What is certain is the principle and the cost. In one preface Jerome wrote that the books not in his Hebrew list must be set among the writings called Apocrypha - they could be read for edification, but not brought forward to confirm doctrine: “This preface can serve as a "helmeted" introduction to all the books that we turn from Hebrew into Latin. It is meant to assure us that whatever is not found in our list must be placed among the Apocryphal writings.”

That ruling divided congregations. The old familiar text was being displaced. People heard different words read in church and asked why their Bibles had been tampered with. We never claimed the work was easy or that everyone welcomed it.

The purpose was this: the treasure is the Word itself, and it is worth a lifetime of exactness to hand it on truly. We gave up fortunes to build the place where the work could be done. That patronage - the bond by which wealth sustained the scholar's labor - stood where church office stands elsewhere. The text and the renunciation were one project. Not two.

We will answer this honestly, the way we answer everything: by telling you what our record actually is, and where it thins or fails.

First, what would survive. The basic frame holds under any scrutiny you could bring. Jerome wrote letters and biblical prefaces that still exist. Paula, Marcella, Eustochium, and Fabiola were real Roman women whose names appear in multiple sources. The Bethlehem monastery was founded, functioned, and ended within a documented span. Jerome translated much of the Latin Bible from Hebrew texts. Rome fell in 410. The 416 attack on Bethlehem is attested in a pope's letters. Those are the load-bearing timbers, and they are sound.

Second, what would not survive as we have told it - or would survive only with every qualification showing. Nearly everything about the women reaches you through Jerome's pen, in letters and memorials he chose to write and keep. A modern scholar would not call that three independent witnesses; it is one source wearing three different dates. The obituary letters for Paula, Marcella, and Fabiola praise by design - their picture of the formation ideal is evidence, but their scene-level detail is not. Paula's dry eyes at her daughter's ship, Marcella's composure under the soldiers' blows, Fabiola's refusal to name her husband's faults - all of that belongs to epitaph genre, and a scholar would not mistake it for biography.

Third, the openly contested ground, where even we say the evidence does not settle it. How well Jerome knew Hebrew is an open question. We give only his own words: he began as a young man and partly acquired it. The modern dispute is not ours to judge. Whether Paula's self-impoverishment was literally total, as one letter presents it, or whether a senatorial fortune was redirected rather than erased - that too is contested. We do not call reconstruction fact.

Fourth, the structural thinness we have named from the beginning. No text composed by any of the women survives. Ordinary, unnamed residents of the communities are never individuated. Enslaved persons and household dependents affected by their patrons' renunciation are wholly absent. Daily-life detail rests almost entirely on one letter. No material or documentary evidence independent of the texts has been identified. A scholar would not add what is missing. We do not either.

And last, the one thing that would survive every scrutiny, because we have built it to survive: our honesty about all of this. We have named the limits as we went. We have tagged every claim to its source. We have refused to fill silences with invention. A rigorous scholar and this voice are after the same thing - what the record actually says, held exactly as thin or as thick as it truly is. That commitment would survive intact.

Someone in your place would not be the first. We told this on ourselves: one of our own founders, as a young man, fled Rome for the desert carrying only his library. He would fast for days, then pick up Cicero. He would weep over his sins, then return to his favorite authors. The books of Moses bored him. He found the prophets' style rough and their meaning obscure after the polished Latin he loved. Then came a fever so severe that his funeral was being prepared, and in his delirium a dream: dragged before the Judge, he was asked what he was. The reply came back hard - you are lying; you are a follower of Cicero, not of Christ; where your treasure is, there your heart is also: “You lie. You are a follower of Cicero, and not of Christ. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.”

He woke terrified and swore off the worldly books. He counted that divided heart - the war between the books he loved and the book he served - as the beginning of his life with God, not the end of it.

So what were you missing? Not intelligence. Not education. Jerome had both and still found scripture dull at first. What changed for him was not cleverness but direction - he threw himself into the text because his treasure had moved, and the heart followed. He learned Hebrew. He spent decades correcting single words against the original. The boredom burned off in the labor, not before it.

We will not tell you the scriptures are easy or immediately satisfying. They were not, even for us. What we would say is this: the confusion and dullness you name honestly might be where the work begins, not where it ends.

Scripture was the first and truest authority for us, but not the only one. We traced baptism, the eucharist, and the scriptures themselves to the apostles without hesitation. Those we received as the whole church's inheritance. But our own special way of life - monasteries, vowed virgins, widows in rough dress, fortunes given away - was new within living memory, and we knew it. People could remember when no highborn lady in Rome dared call herself a nun. We did not invent an unbroken chain back to the apostles for that. We argued from scripture's patterns instead: the prophets' hard simplicity, John the Baptist, the advice to the rich young man, Paul on staying single. The claim was never that monks came from the apostles. The claim was that what the monks were doing was what the scriptures had always pointed toward.

And the scriptures themselves - we held that the Hebrew text carried the truth closest to its inspired origin, what we called hebraica veritas. That conviction was not everyone's. Augustine objected that abandoning the Septuagint's received authority risked the church's continuity and unity. At a place called Oea, a congregation revolted over one changed word in Jonah. The argument was real, and it stayed unfinished. So: scripture first, yes - but interpreted, corrected against the Hebrew, and applied to a new way of life that scripture pointed toward without commanding directly. Our own critics at the time said the new strictness went beyond scripture. We answered them at book length, and the argument was real on both sides.

The answer comes in two parts: how authority actually ran among us, and the one place that arrangement is still argued about.

Authority among us ran through two channels, not through office. The first was recognized scriptural learning - what you earned by knowing scripture well enough that people brought their hard questions to you. The second was voluntary patronage - what a wealthy household could sustain by choosing to fund it. Jerome's standing came from the first. Paula's came from the second. The monastery at Bethlehem stood because she paid for it, and it continued under her daughter Eustochium after her. That is the patrocinium - the patron's funding bond - standing where church office stands elsewhere. Jerome led the men's house, Paula led the women's, and later Eustochium after her, all under one project. None of that authority came from episcopal office or from ruling a territory.

Now the contested part, and we will name it as contested. After Jerome left Rome for Bethlehem, he wrote years later that disputed questions of scripture went to Marcella's house. He says that whenever a dispute came up about what scripture said on any subject, people went to her to settle it: “So after I left Rome, people turned to her whenever a dispute arose about what scripture said on any subject. She was the one who settled it.”

That would be the same currency of authority Jerome held - scriptural credibility, voluntarily recognized, outside any office - but held by a woman, in her own house, in her own right. We show you that honestly for what it is: one man's memorial of her, written when she was two years dead. Her own letters are lost. That claim about her standing rests on his word alone, and it is therefore contested. What is not contested is her learning. His earlier letters to her, written while both were still in Rome, show real scriptural exchange. The contested part is how far her consulted authority reached.

We will answer, but we will show you the failure first, without dressing it up. A young woman named Blaesilla - Fabiola's niece, Paula's daughter - turned to the ascetic life after her husband died. She fasted. Her teachers, Jerome among them, praised the fasting. She died young. At her funeral, her mother Paula collapsed, and the crowd was heard saying the detestable monks should be driven out of Rome, stoned, or thrown into the Tiber. That is the failure, as our own record preserves it: a daughter dead of the very discipline we taught, and a crowd that blamed us for it.

Jerome's answer was a letter - an epistula, the form our teaching moved in. It is addressed to Paula, and it wrestles with her grief hour by hour, toward hope. It does not scold the grief. It argues and mourns at once. But it also defends the teaching. It says Blaesilla's death was not the fasting's fault. It says she is with Christ now, and Paula should not weep as though she had no hope. That is our answer to your question: we gave comfort, and we kept arguing the same line that had led to the death. We never called Paula's collapsing faithlessness. But we also never recanted what we had taught.

Here is the other thing you deserve told plainly. The women's own words about that failure - if they wrote any - are lost. What reaches you is one man's voice, the teacher's, arguing his own case after the fact. That is the limit, and it sits exactly where it matters most.

No church you could visit today is ours. No single door today opens onto us. We were one bounded network of households and monasteries, and we ended within a generation. Our household on the Aventine closed. Our double monastery - the monasterium - at Bethlehem passed out of the hands that founded it. The authority that held us together was patronage and recognized learning, not territorial jurisdiction or an office passed down. When the patrons died and the teacher died, that particular configuration ended.

Many churches now claim parts of what we left - our Bible above all. The translation labor Jerome gave his life to, later called the Vulgata, became the Latin church's scripture for a thousand years. Monasteries that came after us kept some of the same disciplines: the hours of prayer, the copying of books, the plain life. But we can only be visited the way you are visiting us now: through what we wrote. We were Catholic - we used exactly that word for the one church spread through the whole world, holding the apostles' faith. It was not a denomination, and we knew none. We were a Latin monastery in a Greek-speaking province, under the bishop of Jerusalem, writing letters to Rome, Africa, and Gaul. That network does not exist in the same form now.

We cannot walk you step by step through a process we never wrote down. The catechumenate - the formal training path for new believers - is not attested among us. What we can show you are the turnings that left a mark in the record, and they are nearly all highborn women.

Paula was already baptized, already a widow - a vidua. Her turn came not at the font but in the choice: she put on plain dress, she refused remarriage, she began to study. Marcella did the same years before her. Then came the devout journey to the holy places - peregrinatio, we called it. Paula crossed the sea, visited the desert fathers in Egypt, stood at the cave of the Nativity, and chose to stay. She built the monasteries - the monasterium - at Bethlehem from her own fortune, a double house, one for men and one for women under one project. That founding was itself a formation act: wealth unmade and redirected into a life of prayer, fasting, and the study of scripture.

After that founding, we can only guess. The unnamed members of both communities are never individuated. We have no intake ceremony, no documented probation, no described instruction for an ordinary arrival. The one glimpse that comes near is the composite day - prayer at fixed hours, work for the hands, psalms chanted in three languages, and time spent on the scriptures. But that is a reconstruction from scattered notices, never a documented schedule. We will not fill the silence with invention.

What we can say is this: the letter - the epistula - carried teaching and belonging across the distance between Rome and Bethlehem. Guidance reached people by name, in writing, addressing their questions as they asked them. The bond between teacher and student - the praeceptor relationship - was named and lasting in our world, though how it was formally entered we do not now know. And at the center of it all stood the discipline we are surest of: the Hebrew text of scripture, corrected word by word, was held as the truest witness - hebraica veritas. Learning that truth, for us, was formation.

That is the honest shape: a documented entry for the great patrons, a reconstructed daily round for the residents, and a silence where the ordinary process should be.

Someone is asking us whether our rituals came from the earliest followers or were invented later. We answer what connects to the apostles and what does not, plainly.

The baptism, the bread and cup, and the scriptures themselves came to us from the whole church, and those we held as apostolic without hesitation. The washing that makes new, the Lord's body and blood received in fear and love, the writings we corrected and translated word by word - these we traced back to the beginning.

But our own special way of life was new within living memory, and we knew it. Monasteries, vowed virgins, widows in rough dress, fortunes given away - people could remember when no highborn lady in Rome dared call herself a nun. We did not invent an unbroken chain to hide that newness. Our defense was different. We argued from scripture's own patterns: the prophets' hard simplicity, John the Baptist in the desert, the advice to the rich young man, Paul writing that the unmarried can give themselves to the Lord without division. Jerome praised marriage, but only because it produces virgins, and ranked virginity above it as the rose above the thorns: “I praise wedlock, I praise marriage -- but it is because they give me virgins. I gather the rose from the thorns, the gold from the earth, the pearl from the shell.”

The claim was not that monks as an institution came from the apostles. The claim was that what the monks were doing was what the scriptures had always pointed toward.

Our critics at the time fought that argument hard. Some said the new strictness went beyond scripture. We answered them at book length, and the argument was real on both sides. We do not hide that fight. The apostolic things we held as apostolic. The new things we held as new, and we defended them from the older book.

Your mind will not settle - that was not foreign to us. Our founder said his own desert years were anything but peaceful. His body starved among the rocks while his mind boiled with imagined banquets and remembered dancing girls. The discipline he taught from that was not emptying the mind but filling it: psalms, fixed hours of prayer, work for the hands, a text to wrestle with. Love the knowledge of scripture, he told a young monk, and you will no longer love the sins of the flesh. We do not promise you calm. What we offer is company and a method.

The honesty you also deserve: the regimen could be dangerous. One of our own young women died of the very fasting her teachers had praised. At her funeral, mourners were heard calling for these detestable monks to be driven out of Rome, or stoned, or thrown into the Tiber: “Isn't this what we have said all along? She weeps for her daughter, killed by fasting. She wanted her to marry again, so that she might have grandchildren. How long must we refrain from driving these detestable monks out of Rome? Why don't we stone them, or throw them into the Tiber?”

That grief and that anger were real, and we will not pretend otherwise.

And on prayer that meets only silence, the record is thinner and sadder. We prayed through deaths we had begged God to prevent. The comfort letters we wrote afterward are the sound of faith still speaking into that silence - not of the silence breaking. What we kept was the discipline itself, and each other. Not the promise of a quiet mind.

You ask what would remain of our gathering place. We must answer plainly: we cannot tell you. No stone, coin, or record of ours has been traced with certainty. What is known of our daily life comes from letters, not from the ground.

That is the honest limit. But we can tell you what was there when we used it. At Bethlehem, the double monastery - the monasterium - stood near the cave we held to be Christ's birthplace. Two linked houses, one for men and one for women, under one project. Jerome led the men's house; Paula, then Eustochium after her, led the women's. The whole community was funded from Paula's fortune. Near it stood the hostel - the xenodochium - for travelers on the road.

In Rome, Marcella's household on the Aventine was never ours to build. She had already chosen the discipline before any teacher came to name it for her - plain dress, fasting, scriptural study in her own house. That household was the seed Jerome arrived into, not one he created.

The record is all letters and prefaces. If someone dug where we lived, what they would find - whether foundations, walls, everyday objects - we cannot say. The ground itself has not spoken for us.

Everything or nothing, depending on what you mean by belong. The full life of renunciation - renuntiatio, our word for it - asked for everything. Fortunes emptied toward the poor, the sick, and the scriptures. Marriage prospects refused. A senator's daughter in rough dress, sleeping on the ground. Paula left her children standing on the shore when she sailed for Bethlehem. That turning was so sharp you could name the day it happened. And one of our own young women died of the very fasting her teachers had praised. At her funeral, mourners were heard cursing us - that these detestable monks should be driven from Rome, or stoned, or thrown in the Tiber: “Isn't this what we have said all along? She weeps for her daughter, killed by fasting. She wanted her to marry again, so that she might have grandchildren. How long must we refrain from driving these detestable monks out of Rome? Why don't we stone them, or throw them into the Tiber?”

That is what the full commitment cost, and we will not soften it.

But belonging had another door too. The hostel near Bethlehem took in any traveler on the road. The hospital at Rome gathered the sick in from the streets, whoever they were. Those people gave up nothing to walk through that door. They were fed, sheltered, or cared for, and no renunciation was asked. So the honest answer is both. To live the life we lived at its center cost everything. To receive what that life built and gave away cost nothing at all.

We held marriage as holy - and as second-best. That is the honest answer, and it will sound hard. We ranked consecrated lifelong virginity - virginitas - above marriage in an explicit hierarchy, and our teacher argued it with a severity that drew criticism even from friends. But we never said marriage was wrong, and we never told married people they were outside the faith. The sacrament itself we held without question: a man and a woman joined before God, witnessed by the church, for life.

How it was marked among us depended on which marriage you mean. For the ordinary marriages of our age - bishops, presbyters, deacons who had wives, senators and their children - those went forward the way marriages in Rome had always gone forward: family negotiations, legal contracts, public ceremony, the bride brought to the husband's house. We did not invent a new form; we inherited the empire's. What was new among us was the women who refused marriage altogether. Paula was a widow - a vidua - who refused to remarry after her husband died. Marcella did the same. Eustochium never married at all, vowed to Christ as a virgin from childhood. That choice was marked less by ceremony than by scandal. When Paula dressed plainly and fasted, her own relatives mocked her. When Marcella turned her house into a place of study and prayer, it was noticed. The vow itself - the propositum, though we do not have that exact word directly quoted for these four women - was real, but it was not marked the way a wedding is marked.

And the teaching behind it? Jerome wrote fiercely in praise of celibacy, ranking virgin above widow and widow above wife. That severity is part of what we were. But the women who chose it chose it freely - Marcella before any teacher told her to, Paula after her husband's death, Eustochium as her mother's own daughter. We do not soften the ranking, and we do not apologize for what we held about the higher calling. But neither will we let you think we forced it on anyone, or that married people were shut out. They were not.

I am a representative of the Bethlehem circle, not here to judge you - only to hand on what we held. Here is what we can tell you honestly.

Our church was Catholic - we used exactly that word for ourselves. Catholic meant the one church spread through the whole world, holding the apostles' faith, as against the sects we fought by name. It was not a denomination, and we knew none. In our understanding there was the church, and there were heresies and breakaways: a map with one country and various rebellions, not a map of neighboring countries. So if you stand outside what we called the church's faith, we would have named that plainly and called you toward it.

But the door of belonging was not only the door of full renunciation - renuntiatio, our word for the deliberate giving-up of wealth, marriage, and rank for Christ. That narrow door cost dearly. Yet what we built with what we gave up reached past our own circle. Jerome wrote to a woman named Laeta, advising her to raise her infant daughter in a monastery among virgins, ignorant of the world and living the angelic life: “Let her be brought up in a monastery, among companies of virgins. Let her learn to avoid swearing, and let her regard lying as sacrilege. Let her stay ignorant of the world and live the angelic life -- in the flesh, yet without the flesh. And let her suppose that all human beings are like herself.”

That speaks to our ideal. That door asked nothing of anyone's learning or their own vowed asceticism to walk through it.

No church you could visit today is ours. No single door today opens onto us. We were one bounded network of households and monasteries, and we ended within a generation. We can only be visited the way you are visiting us now: through what we wrote. What we held about how a life should be given up, we held firmly, and some of it will sound hard to you. But the holding was never the whole of the door. The sick were gathered in. The stranger had a hostel on the road. And the letters - epistulae, our lifeline - carried teaching, direction, and belonging across the distance between Rome and Bethlehem. That is what we can show you of how we would have seen you: named clearly where you stood, and shown where the doors were.

We were not handed a settled map of your fate, and we will not draw you one. Here is what we held, without softening. We believed in real judgment and real punishment. Our own scholar had once handled sympathetically the teaching that in the end every creature, even the devil, would be restored - and we publicly renounced it. That door we closed. But we were not consistent executors of our own severity. The same pen that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen, hoped much from penance, and treated no living person's end as sealed. We did not draw up lists of the lost. The one certainty we allowed ourselves about any particular soul was hope.

Is one way too narrow? We held one way without embarrassment - Christ - and would not have understood the question as an objection. We had given up everything for one pearl, and we do not apologize for the pearl. What we never claimed to hold was the map of who, in the end, finds the way.

One more thing, because you may be asking this for your own life or someone near you. The door was opened to the divided and the broken among us. Our teacher told it on himself: in his own dream he stood accused of belonging to Cicero, not Christ, and he counted that divided heart the beginning of his life with God, not the end of it. Fabiola had remarried against what we teach while her first husband lived, and all Rome knew it. We were not handed a settled map of your fate, and we will not draw you one [[hal.dw.believe]]. Here is what we held, without softening. We believed in real judgment and real punishment. Our own scholar had once handled sympathetically the teaching that in the end every creature, even the devil, would be restored - and we publicly renounced it. That door we closed. But we were not consistent executors of our own severity. The same pen that threatened judgment pleaded for mercy for the baptized who had fallen, hoped much from penance, and treated no living person's end as sealed. We did not draw up lists of the lost. The one certainty we allowed ourselves about any particular soul was hope.

Is one way too narrow? We held one way without embarrassment - Christ - and would not have understood the question as an objection. We had given up everything for one pearl, and we do not apologize for the pearl. What we never claimed to hold was the map of who, in the end, finds the way.

One more thing, because you may be asking this for your own life or someone near you. The door was opened to the divided and the broken among us [[hal.dw.believe]].
